note.text: Cameroon’s vegetation includes humid southern forests, savannah mosaics, drier northern formations, montane communities and coastal mangroves. These are broad patterns with transitions rather than perfectly straight boundaries. Moisture, temperature, soil, drainage and disturbance interact. Forests can be evergreen or semi-deciduous depending on conditions; savannah has variable woody cover. Montane vegetation responds to altitude, while mangroves occupy suitable tidal settings. Farms, settlements, logging and fire can replace or modify natural formations, creating secondary vegetation and mosaics.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to relate major vegetation formations to climate altitude drainage and human modification. Builds on: biomes and Cameroon’s climatic contrasts. Leads to: soil patterns and later ecosystem and land-use evaluation.

sections.heading: Explain the geography
sections.text: Cameroon’s vegetation includes humid southern forests, savannah mosaics, drier northern formations, montane communities and coastal mangroves. These are broad patterns with transitions rather than perfectly straight boundaries. Moisture, temperature, soil, drainage and disturbance interact. Forests can be evergreen or semi-deciduous depending on conditions; savannah has variable woody cover. Montane vegetation responds to altitude, while mangroves occupy suitable tidal settings. Farms, settlements, logging and fire can replace or modify natural formations, creating secondary vegetation and mosaics.

sections.heading: Follow the local example or model
sections.text: Compare forest in southern Cameroon, seasonal savannah farther north and cooler vegetation on high western slopes. A moist gallery along a stream can differ from the surrounding landscape. Mangroves near an estuary reflect salinity and tidal conditions as well as rainfall. A satellite image’s green colour alone does not distinguish plantation, young regrowth and intact forest; local records and field identification are needed.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Explain pattern at both regional and local scale. Use climate together with altitude, drainage and land-use history. Distinguish potential natural vegetation from present cover. A boundary can be gradual or disturbed rather than a fixed line. Classroom interpretation does not require entering a protected site or collecting plants.

pick.q: A humid southern forest patch is cleared, then shrubs and young trees regrow.
pick.r: The regrowth may be secondary vegetation shaped by disturbance.
w: The region instantly becomes a permanent hot desert.
Every young tree proves untouched primary forest.
No human activity can affect plant cover.
e: Clearing alone does not establish a new desert climate.
Regrowth after clearing differs from undisturbed mature structure.
The stated clearing directly changes the cover.
pick.y: Use land-use history with climate and site evidence.

pick.q: A tidal coastal site has waterlogged saline or brackish conditions.

e: Alpine settings are high-altitude, unlike this site.
Tidal salinity identifies a different site constraint.
Salinity and tidal conditions influence the plant community.
pick.y: Describe the habitat conditions before predicting vegetation.

pick.q: An upland site is cooler and more exposed than nearby lowland forest.
pick.r: Altitude and exposure can support a different montane plant community.
w: Higher ground must have the same plants at every elevation.
Only longitude changes vegetation at a site.
A cooler site proves the country lies outside the tropics.
e: Temperature and exposure can change with altitude.
Altitude and local conditions are relevant here.
High elevations can be cool within a tropical country.
pick.y: Altitude modifies local conditions without moving the country’s latitude.

pick.q: A river corridor stays moister than surrounding seasonal grassland.
pick.r: Gallery vegetation may follow the better-watered corridor.
w: The corridor proves every surrounding slope is equally moist.
Rivers cannot influence nearby plants.
All vegetation boundaries must follow administrative borders.
e: A local water supply differs from the regional upland setting.
Available moisture affects plant communities.
Ecological conditions do not have to match administrative lines.
pick.y: Separate local corridor conditions from the wider landscape.
